source: Unbounce, Michael Aagaard, failed A/B tests post
variant_a: Payment-page button in first person: '... My ...' (control; full button text not given)
variant_b: Same button in second person: '... Your ...'
metric: clicks on the payment button (final funnel step)
why_it_won: Source: Aagaard expected 'your' to win because sites address visitors in second person; it lost and he offers no mechanism. Our reading: on an order form the reader is already acting as 'I', so first-person button copy mirrors the decision being made.
principle: Sec 9 order form: button states the buyer's action; Sec 9 opt-in: button completes 'I want...'. Supports first-person CTA copy.
verification_note: Verified 2026-10-24. Body text states -24.95%; the article's own headline says -26.55%. Figure kept as the body text states it.

source: Unbounce, Michael Aagaard, failed A/B tests post
variant_b: Get my free 30-day trial
metric: CTR on PPC landing page button (unbounce.com)
why_it_won: Source: cited as the largest of several 'my' vs 'your' tests, no mechanism given. Our reading: two variables changed at once ('my' and 'free'), so the lift cannot be attributed to person alone.
principle: Sec 9 opt-in page: button completing 'I want...'. Supports first-person CTA, with a confound (added 'free').

source: Unbounce, Michael Aagaard, failed A/B tests post (Bettingexpert.com)
variant_a: Sign-up form with no privacy line (control)
variant_b: Form plus '100% privacy – We will never spam you'
why_it_won: Source: the word 'spam' next to the form planted the fear it denied.
principle: Sec 9 opt-in page must-not: 'we will never spam you.' Directly supports the rule.

source: Unbounce, Michael Aagaard, failed A/B tests post (Bettingexpert.com follow-up)
variant_a: Form with no privacy line / earlier 'spam' wording (baseline not named explicitly)
variant_b: We guarantee 100% privacy. Your information will not be shared.
why_it_won: Source: removing the word 'spam' fixed the problem found in the prior test; a positive privacy promise reassures without naming the fear.
principle: Sec 9 opt-in: no 'we will never spam you'; Sec 4 proof/reassurance stated as a positive promise. Supports.

source: Unbounce, Michael Aagaard, failed A/B tests post (CRO e-book landing page)
variant_b: 100% privacy – I will never spam you!
why_it_won: Source: same pattern as the Bettingexpert test; naming spam near the form reduces conversions.
principle: Sec 9 opt-in must-not 'we will never spam you'. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #146625, American Cornerstone Institute
variant_a: Post-pledge donation page headline thanking the visitor for signing the pledge (control wording shown only as image)
variant_b: Your name has been added. Before you go, would you consider this special request from Dr. Ben Carson? (T2 also rewrote body in first person, signed by the founder)
lift: +114.0% conversion rate (T2); headline alone +95.4% at 93.3% confidence
why_it_won: Source: the continuation headline pulled visitors into the value proposition; first-person copy signed by a named messenger created a stronger connection.
principle: Sec 3 most-aware/returning: line one continues the decision just made; Sec 9 upsell/OTO: one-line confirmation of the first decision then bridge. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #2302, Texas State Historical Association
variant_a: Do you love Texas history? Join the Texas State Historical Association today!
variant_b: Get insider access to the most exclusive Texas History Club in the Nation
lift: -65.0% conversion rate for the treatment (key learnings say -62% donors)
why_it_won: Source (Tim Kachuriak): the treatment added benefit language but lost clarity about what the page was for; 'added value while losing clarity'.
principle: Sec 2 C7 one-sentence clarity and C9 claim <= proof: an unsupported superlative ('most exclusive ... in the Nation') with no carrier lost to a plain statement of purpose. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #3666, CaringBridge tribute funnel
variant_b: Personalized, donor-centric headline reminding the visitor of the impact of their gift (wording only in image)
why_it_won: Source (Jeff Giddens): reminding visitors of the gift's impact appeared to help in a funnel tied to a personal relationship; result tentative.
principle: Sec 2 C11 important/exciting/beneficial in the reader's terms. Weakly supports; underpowered.

source: NextAfter experiment #31412, Compassion International
variant_a: Help a child keep their sponsor!
variant_b: Same headline with 'child' and 'sponsor' swapped so the sponsor is the beneficiary (exact wording not shown)
why_it_won: Source (Jeff Giddens): sponsors may empathize with fellow sponsors more than with the immediate needs of a child; more testing needed.
principle: Sec 2 C4 awareness fit / C5 right problem: the headline must name the reader's own problem, not the writer's. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #2724, Illinois Policy Institute
variant_a: Main donation page with only a headline and the form
variant_b: Same page plus value-proposition copy explaining what the organization does and why to give
why_it_won: Source: the team had assumed visitors on the donation page were already committed; a clear value proposition motivated far more to give.
principle: Sec 9 order form/short landing page: argued benefits with proof in line; Sec 1 claim/reason/proof. Supports: do not assume the page's visitor is sold.

source: NextAfter experiment #3520, Harvest Ministries
variant_b: donate
metric: clickthrough on homepage premium block (0.50% vs 0.82%)
why_it_won: Source: visitors arrive with some motivation to give and are not repelled by a direct ask.
principle: Sec 9 CTA as verb/object; Sec 3 most-aware gets the offer in line one. Supports direct asks over disguised ones.

source: NextAfter experiment #3525, Harvest Ministries (conversion follow-through)
variant_b: donate
lift: +104.6% conversion rate on the following page
why_it_won: Source: 'clarity is king'; 'get your copy' reads as bait-and-switch once a donation is required, 'donate' sets expectations.
principle: Sec 8 claims: offer stated exactly as it is; Sec 9 order form: nothing the close did not state. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #7496, Focus on the Family
variant_b: Get Your Resource for a Gift of Any Amount Here (T2: For a Gift of Any Amount, Get Your Resource Here)
why_it_won: Source: the button told donors both what they receive and how they receive it, reducing friction; an earlier 'Get the DVD Here' drove traffic but lowered conversion because visitors expected the resource free.
principle: Sec 9 order bump: 'Yes! Add [thing] for only $X' (what and the price in the button). Supports stating the exchange in the CTA.

source: NextAfter experiment #3318, Focus on the Family broadcast page
variant_b: Get Your CD Here (image labelled 'Get Your Resource Here')
lift: +64.7% clicks to the donation page; donor conversion then fell about 4%
metric: click rate to donation page (2.0% vs 3.3%)
why_it_won: Source: visitors were more motivated to get the resource than to give; the stronger button weakened the donation-for-resource expectation downstream.
principle: Sec 9 order form: no claim the close did not state. A CTA that hides the exchange buys clicks and loses conversions. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #203230, Minnesota Public Radio (The Thread)
variant_b: Copy stating the newsletter's value and what readers can expect (image only)
lift: +336.7% downstream transactions; email sign-ups +6.5% at 60% confidence
why_it_won: Source (Jeff Giddens): modest lift in sign-ups, the significant gain came downstream on the donation page; recommends value-focused copy on sign-up pages.
principle: Sec 9 opt-in page: incomplete bullets and one proof line; Sec 1 the skim path sells alone. Supports (but the headline metric is downstream).
verification_note: Verified 2026-10-24. Source results table attributes +336.7% to landing-page conversion rate while Key Learnings attribute it to downstream transactions; the source does not reconcile the two.

source: NextAfter experiment #201112, Human Coalition year-end donation page
variant_a: You can give to rescue moms and babies from abortion starting right now
variant_b: You can be the reason a mom cancels her abortion appointment
why_it_won: Source: a specific, immediate outcome tied to the reader's action felt more personally impactful; it may have attracted lower-dollar donors.
principle: Sec 2 C7 one sentence, eight words or fewer, concrete picture; Sec 1 precision. Supports on conversion, cautions on revenue: the metric decides.
verification_note: Verified 2026-10-24 (experiment #201112). Table confidence 97.3%; summary text says 97.2%.

source: NextAfter experiment #202191, Minnesota Public Radio premium offer
variant_b: Same page offering a Public Media Advocacy T-shirt for $5 monthly or $60 one-time
why_it_won: Source: the premium paired the mission ask with a thank-you; growth came mainly from recurring giving.
principle: Sec 5 offer presentation / Sec 9 stack: a tangible premium tied to a specific threshold. Supports.
verification_note: Verified 2026-10-24 (experiment #202191). Results table states +131.9% conversion; Key Learnings state +34.3% overall transactions at 94% confidence. Monthly gifts +102.9%, revenue +215.3% confirmed.

source: NextAfter experiment #202797, CaringBridge single post page
variant_b: Widget with educational language explaining what a tribute gift is and does
why_it_won: Source: clearer information and less friction about what the gift is increased donations.
principle: Sec 2 C10 mechanism named and explained; Sec 9 order form 'what arrives and when'. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #12712, The Heritage Foundation
variant_b: Long-form donor-centered appeal
lift: -37.8% conversion rate; average gift +61.3%; revenue -0.6% (NOT VALID, 94.8%)
why_it_won: Source: researcher hypothesizes copy length caused the drop; higher average gift was encouraging, so a short donor-centered version is planned.
principle: Sec 3 most-aware traffic: offer lead, do not explain the problem. Supports: long copy on a primary donate page serving warm traffic.

source: NextAfter experiment #2989, Focus on the Family recurring gift page
variant_a: Transactional copy describing what donors receive
variant_b: Value proposition copy explaining what the monthly gift will do
lift: +31.5% conversion rate; average gift about -4.7% ($60.51 vs $57.66)
why_it_won: Source (Courtney Gaines): what the gift does motivated more than what the donor receives.
principle: Sec 1 benefits as claim, reason, proof, picture; Sec 2 C11 beneficial in reader's terms. Supports.
verification_note: Verified 2026-10-24. Corrected: source reports average gift $60.51 (control) vs $57.66 (treatment), about -4.7%, described as 'slightly higher' for the control, not unchanged.

source: NextAfter experiment #10464, Boys Town primary donation page
variant_a: Control banner: 'Thank you, you're not just saving one child' (per summary)
variant_b: Banner with a stronger case for support and the donor's impact
why_it_won: Source: visitors to this page have varied motivations (many from direct mail); the stronger value proposition lowered conversion for the whole, lifted new mobile visitors.
principle: Sec 3: most-aware traffic (direct-mail responders) wants the offer, not re-education. Supports the awareness-first rule; contradicts 'more value prop always wins'.

source: NextAfter experiment #10908, NextAfter benchmark report enrollment
variant_a: 'What You Get' framing: data is being gathered for a new benchmark study (image only)
variant_b: 'Why It's Valuable' value-first framing (image only)
why_it_won: Source: value-heavy copy blurred what the offer was and implied an immediate download the form did not deliver.
principle: Sec 9 opt-in must-not 'headline describing the artifact' is nuanced here: clarity about the exchange beat benefit talk. Supports Sec 2 C7 clarity; cautions against benefit copy that misstates the offer.

source: NextAfter experiment #204554, American Cornerstone Institute
variant_b: Same copy plus monthly partner benefits listed, with monthly giving preselected
why_it_won: Source: highlighting monthly benefits and preselecting monthly 'subtly influenced donors towards monthly giving'; trade-off against one-time gifts.
principle: Sec 5 offer presentation: options highest-value first, default framed. Supports with the trade-off recorded.

source: NextAfter experiment #204013, Dallas Theological Seminary
variant_a: Post-registration page led with 'Story of Scripture Registration Confirmation' and 'Thank You!' before the donation ask
variant_b: Confirmation and thank-you removed; congratulatory message and donation invitation became the top message
why_it_won: Source: copy that only confirmed a completed action was removed, moving visitors faster from registration to the opportunity to give.
principle: Sec 9 thank-you page / upsell: one-line confirmation then bridge to the next offer; close at 15-25% of length. Supports cutting dead confirmation copy.

source: NextAfter experiment #66578, e3 Partners prayer pledge (Facebook)
variant_a: Control header reiterating that the visitor just signed the pledge
variant_b: New value-proposition copy moving from the pledge to e3's mission
why_it_won: Source: the control's reminder of the action just taken likely drove conversion; new copy to be rewritten and retested.
principle: Sec 9 upsell/OTO: confirm the first decision and bridge from it; do not re-educate. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #1956, Texas State Historical Association membership form
variant_a: Long copy explaining mission, history and membership benefits
variant_b: Short form with substantially reduced copy
lift: +0.5% for short form, i.e. no difference (NOT VALID)
metric: donor conversion rate (5.2% vs 5.2%); average gift $51.60 vs $62.00 n.s.
why_it_won: Source: copy length 'is not a significant factor' on this page; add value through propositions and incentives instead.
principle: Sec 9: bands are starting values, the control overrides them. Neutral on length; supports testing argument over length.

source: NextAfter experiment #98763, FamilyLife premium offer page
variant_b: 154-word version of the same value proposition
lift: +204.1% revenue per visitor ($0.51 to $1.54); average gift +150.4%; conversion +21.4% not validated
why_it_won: Source: shorter copy reduced friction on mobile, the primary device; lift held across device and visitor segments.
principle: Sec 9 short landing page 150-600 words for product-aware traffic; Sec 3 product-aware gets promise, not re-education. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #3950, exit-intent offer on webinar landing pages
variant_b: Condensed copy in a smaller pop-up
why_it_won: Source (Nathan Hill): the short copy had less specific and clear detail about what visitors would receive.
principle: Sec 1 precision; Sec 9 opt-in: incomplete bullets with specifics. Supports: cut words, never cut specifics.

source: NextAfter experiment #10649, The Leadership Institute
variant_b: Longer copy detailing the adversity and how the gift stops it
why_it_won: Source: longer copy is acceptable if it explains how the donor's gift can stop the problem.
principle: Sec 9 long-form: problem mechanism then solution mechanism; Sec 2 C10. Supports.

source: NextAfter experiment #2690, FamilyLife primary donation page
variant_a: Large hero image with traditional value proposition copy
variant_b: Radical redesign: new value proposition copy, other elements removed
why_it_won: Source (Courtney Gaines): less friction plus stronger value proposition brought more donors at a higher gift; not statistically reliable.
principle: Sec 1 claim/reason/proof. Weak support; underpowered.

source: NextAfter experiment #2092, Jews for Jesus
variant_a: Donation link in navigation only (control); T2 'Donate Today!' button
variant_b: 'Make my Gift' header button
lift: +74.0% donation conversion for 'Make my Gift'; 'Donate Today!' -6.0% at 15.6%
why_it_won: Source: first-person framing aligned with donor intent; the command 'Donate Today!' reduced traffic.
principle: Sec 9: button completes 'I want...'; CTA as verb+object. Supports first-person CTA over imperative-with-urgency.

source: NextAfter experiment #2361, Alliance Defending Freedom blog
variant_a: Blog posts with no calls to action
variant_b: Generic donate and subscribe CTAs added at the bottom
why_it_won: Source: 'just adding the calls to action' did not inspire readers; next step is to contextualize the CTA to the content and emphasize one primary CTA.
principle: Sec 9 organic/content: a sales intent inside the content, one CTA with verb/object/location. Supports: an uncontextualized CTA is dead weight.

source: NextAfter experiment #173690, Heritage Foundation / The Daily Signal
variant_a: News site header with no donate button
variant_b: Header 'Donate' button (T2 branded with gift icon)
lift: +2,694% clicks to donation page (from near zero); donor conversion -9.3% (14.5% conf.) / -64% near-valid
why_it_won: Source: people who click a prominent button may be less motivated than those who seek out the page.
principle: Sec 3: traffic state governs the lead; a button that changes who arrives must change the page. Supports awareness-first.

source: NextAfter experiment #90357, I Am Second
variant_b: Headline rewritten to the value proposition, donor-centric body, navigation removed, different platform
lift: stated inconsistently: +8.7% conversion in summary, 100.0% relative difference in table
why_it_won: Source: changes were deliberately radical; recommends re-running on one platform. Our reading: confounded multi-variable test, low traffic.
principle: Sec 2 C12 inevitable conclusion. Weak support; confounded.

source: NextAfter blog, 8 A/B tests to try on your donation page (test 8)
variant_a: No text below the donate button
variant_b: One sentence below the button reinforcing the value of giving
why_it_won: Source: a reassurance at the moment of decision. Our reading: proof/value within two sentences of the ask.
principle: Sec 4 proof placement: proof within two sentences of the claim; Sec 9 order form: guarantee beside the button. Supports.

source: NextAfter blog, 8 A/B tests to try on your donation page (test 5)
variant_b: Conversational, welcoming copy that emphasizes the reader
why_it_won: Source: 'communal' language speaking to the reader rather than about the organization.
principle: Sec 7 AI tell: assistant/brand voice; Sec 1: one reader. Supports.

source: NextAfter blog, 8 A/B tests to try on your donation page (test 4)
variant_a: Donation page with a video carrying the message
variant_b: Video removed, same message delivered as copy
why_it_won: Source: the copy carried the same message without the friction of pressing play.
principle: Sec 1 the skim path sells alone. Supports copy over gated media on the decision page.

source: VWO (Wingify) success story, Movexa
variant_a: Original headline without the product category word (image only)
variant_b: Same headline with the word 'supplement' added
why_it_won: Source: adding 'supplement' let visitors grasp what Movexa is without reading the full copy. Vendor-published, self-reported.
principle: Sec 2 C7 clarity in one sentence; Sec 3 solution-aware: name the category. Supports.

source: VWO (Wingify) success story, LKR Social Media / Laura Roeder
variant_a: Could You Use a Free Plan For Promoting With Social Media?
variant_b: Yours is the only newsletter that I actually read.
why_it_won: Source: headline taken from real, frequent customer feedback; 'do something different that gets attention'. Vendor-published.
principle: Sec 2: lead verbatim from the customer; Sec 9 opt-in: one proof line. Supports testimonial-as-headline; question headline lost.

source: VWO (Wingify) success story, AwayFind
variant_a: Headline 'Checking email every 5 minutes? Stop!' with extended headline 'Let us find your urgent messages.'
variant_b: Second headline replaced by a sub-headline and layout drawing the eye to the CTA (wording in image)
why_it_won: Source: more compelling copy and a layout that led to the button; follow-up planned to isolate copy from layout. Confounded.
principle: Sec 9 short landing page: headline, subhead with who and differentiator, CTA. Weak support (confounded).

source: VWO (Wingify) success story, Imsider.ru
variant_a: A step-by-step plan for opening your internet store (translated from Russian)
variant_b: Open your internet store in one evening (translated from Russian)
why_it_won: Source: a time-bound promise, a sense the task is easy, and a command verb opening appealed to first-timers who assume it is hard and slow.
principle: Sec 9 opt-in: headline with number, timeframe or mechanism, not describing the artifact. Supports.

source: VWO (Wingify) success story, Veeam Software
variant_b: Request pricing
why_it_won: Source: a survey showed visitors wanted pricing; the link label that named what they wanted won. Lead-volume impact not shown.
principle: Sec 9 B2B pricing page must-not: gated pricing without a stated reason; CTA names what the reader gets. Supports.

source: VWO (Wingify) blog, PriceCharting.com
variant_a: Download Sega Genesis Price List for $2 (button 'Download', fee beside it)
variant_b: Download Sega Genesis Price Guide (button 'Price Guide', price removed)
why_it_won: Source: 'Download' plus a price looked like a banner ad; the winner was more relevant (visitors wanted a price guide) and more specific. Follow-up with 'Starts at $4' did not beat it.
principle: Sec 9 CTA as verb + object; Sec 5 price after value. Supports; note the price-removal confound.

source: Conversion Rate Experts, Crazy Egg case study
variant_b: Redesigned page about 20x longer answering visitors' questions
why_it_won: Source: 'length is not the problem; a page that is too boring is'; visitors wanted their questions answered.
principle: Sec 9 long-form: the skim path sells alone, objections answered; Sec 3 solution-aware gets the mechanism. Supports.

source: Conversion Rate Experts, Crazy Egg case study (checkout)
variant_a: Free-trial sign-up with no explanation of why a card is required or how billing works
variant_b: Explanation box under the button: no charge during the trial, yearly billing and cancellation terms clarified
why_it_won: Source: visitors thought the card request was a scam and were confused by monthly vs yearly; confusion causes hesitation.
principle: Sec 9 order form: price, total and every added cost; what arrives and when; guarantee beside the button. Supports.
verification_note: Verified 2026-10-24. Source states +116% signups for the revised checkout page as a whole and does not isolate the explanation box; other changes (yearly billing terms clarified) shipped in the same variant.

source: Conversion Rate Experts, Smart Insights case study
variant_a: Visitors sent straight to the membership pricing page
variant_b: New pre-pricing sales page: offer, appeals and objections, price anchored against a personal consultation, member benefits listed
why_it_won: Source: newcomers met pricing too soon; showing the offer first and anchoring against expert consultation brought them up to speed.
principle: Sec 9 B2B pricing: value argument restated above the price, anchor against the expensive alternative; Sec 5 price after value. Supports.

source: Conversion Rate Experts, Smart Insights case study (sign-up form)
variant_b: Two-part form with new headline and sidebar of appeals and proof; non-essential fields moved to post-signup wizard
why_it_won: Source: visitors needed reassurance of instant access, objections answered at the form, fewer fields.
principle: Sec 9 order form: eight fields or fewer, trust block in the payment area, recap in the close's words. Supports.

source: Conversion Rate Experts, Moz (SEOmoz) case study
variant_a: Short page, headline 'Improve your traffic and rankings with an SEOmoz PRO Membership!'
variant_b: Page ~6x longer, headline 'When eBay, Disney, and Marriott need SEO help, here's what they do…' plus tier chart, Q&A, logos, testimonials, CEO video
why_it_won: Source: the long page told the story the CEO told in person; a curiosity headline held attention before selling; proof the company took for granted was made prominent.
principle: Sec 3 solution-aware: Secret/Promise lead with proof; Sec 9 long-form proof block. Supports.

source: Conversion Rate Experts, guarantees article (Geeks2U test 1a)
variant_b: Written guarantee formalizing the service features customers already praised (wording in image)
why_it_won: Source: the guarantee works as a promise, not just a get-out clause.
principle: Sec 9 long-form and order form: guarantee verbatim beside the button; Sec 5 risk reversal. Supports.

source: Conversion Rate Experts, guarantees article (Geeks2U test 1b)
variant_b: More specific and more prominent guarantee
why_it_won: Source implies specificity and prominence strengthened the effect over test 1a.
principle: Sec 1 precision matches the evidence; specific promises beat vague ones. Supports.

source: Conversion Rate Experts, guarantees article (Geeks2U test 2)
variant_b: One striking sentence phrased as a positive promise with a simple visual, e.g. 'We guarantee that you'll love our service.'
lift: +24% over the previous winner; +49% calls to sales vs the guarantee-less original
why_it_won: Source: mouse-movement maps showed the guarantee was among the most-read elements; positive-promise framing and concision won.
principle: Sec 9 upsell: one-line guarantee; Sec 5. Supports.

source: Copyhackers, Amazon review mining (Beachway)
variant_b: If you think you need rehab, you do.
lift: >400% more clicks on the CTA; >20% more lead-form submits on the next page
why_it_won: Source (Joanna Wiebe): the headline is a reviewer's exact sentence from 500+ Amazon reviews of addiction books; no later treatment has beaten it.
principle: Sec 2: lead verbatim and the belief to displace; Sec 3 problem-aware: name the need in the reader's words. Supports.

source: Unbounce guest post by Joanna Wiebe, testimonial-swiped headline (SaaS client)
variant_a: Control headline (image only); losing marketer-written variant 2: 'End the headache of constantly emailing files & appointment requests back and forth' (-11.8%)
variant_b: Headline and subhead adapted from a customer testimonial found on the client's site (image only)
lift: +103% clicks to Plans & Pricing; three of four treatments lost, one by -100%
metric: clicks from landing page to Plans & Pricing
why_it_won: Source: customer language outperformed the copywriter's own treatments.
principle: Sec 2 lead verbatim; Sec 10 voice capture from the customer corpus. Supports.

source: Copyhackers, Crazy Egg home page case study
variant_b: Four copy treatments by Copyhackers (wording in video)
lift: +13% for the best of four treatments
why_it_won: Source gives no explanation on the page; details are in a video case study.
principle: Sec 6: predicts beat/lose against a control; small gains on a strong control. Neutral.

source: Copyhackers, MetaGeek text link vs buttons
variant_b: Four button treatments with headers, value/urgency cues, horizontal comparison, enlarged CTAs, lead form (B -6%, C -14%, D -20%, E -80%)
why_it_won: Source hypotheses: big attractive buttons on a download site look like spam/scam; headers made visitors notice Office is not free; D and E added form friction.
principle: Sec 6: never repair a higher failure (trust/offer clarity) lower down (button design). Supports.

source: Copyhackers, clear vs clever headline (JCD Repair)
variant_a: Default clear headline (image only; scored 30/50 by the authors)
variant_b: Variation 3, light St. Patrick's Day humour tied to the client's biggest sales day (image only; scored 41/50)
why_it_won: Source: humour tied to a real timing hook beat the embarrassment angle and the plain default.
principle: Sec 2 C6 timing evidence (a named event); Sec 9 SMS must-not jokes is format-specific. Partial support: the hook was a dated event, not cleverness for its own sake.

source: Copyhackers, Mad Mimi pricing page A/B/C
variant_a: Plan buttons 'Sign Up!', plans Basic/Pro/Silver/Gold, infinity symbols
variant_b: C: 'Get Started', least expensive first, 'unlimited' spelled out, 'premium support' added (B: 'Get Started Now', Silver first, Gold moved to text)
lift: 'massive lift' on every plan goal, not stated numerically; C beat B except on Gold
why_it_won: Source hypotheses: price-sensitive visitors; leading with $199 signalled 'too expensive'; the Gold plan made $10 look like a bargain.
principle: Sec 9 B2B pricing: three plans, anchor against the expensive alternative, 'Best for [persona]'. Partial support; CONTRADICTS Sec 9 order form 'options highest price first' for this audience.

source: CXL, Truckers Report case study (test 4, headline)
variant_a: Get a truck driving job with better pay.
variant_b: You can get a driving job with better pay. But, of course, you are free to choose. (also tested: 'Looking for a truck driving job with better pay?' and 'Better Pay. More Benefits. Respect for drivers.')
lift: control beat the best challenger by 16.2%; all three variations lost
why_it_won: Source: 'simple and straightforward worked best'; the question and three-benefit headlines also lost.
principle: Sec 2 C7 eight words, no qualifier; Sec 9 ads must-not 'Are you tired of' question openers. Supports.

source: CXL, Truckers Report case study (test 2, headline + benefit bullets)
variant_b: New headline and benefit bullets built from survey wording (image only)
lift: no difference in opt-ins; control won bottom-of-funnel completions by 21.7%
why_it_won: Source: 'too many promises can look like hype'; big promises drew people less motivated to finish.
principle: Sec 1 claim never bigger than proof; Sec 2 C9. Supports: VOC words alone do not license bigger promises.

source: CXL, Truckers Report case study (test 5, shorter page)
variant_b: Shorter page with less copy
why_it_won: Source: shorter layouts with less copy increased opt-ins for this audience (mobile ~50% of traffic).
principle: Sec 9 opt-in page 60-250 words. Supports.

source: CXL, Truckers Report case study (test 1, form fields)
variant_b: Fewer form fields
lift: control beat the shorter form by 13.56%
why_it_won: Source guess: extra fields add credibility; a bare email field can look 'spammy'.
principle: Sec 9 opt-in: email-only form. CONTRADICTS the default for this audience; the control overrides the band.

source: CXL, Truckers Report case study (test 6, final design and field order)
variant_b: Compact design, email the only required field, no name field, easy fields first and email last
lift: +44.7% opt-ins; cumulative 12.1% to 21.7% (+79.3%) over six rounds
why_it_won: Source: easy fields first then email may build commitment and consistency.
principle: Sec 9 opt-in: email-only; eight fields or fewer. Supports.
